chunks: Abu Basir said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about what falls into wells. He said: 'As for the rat and its likes, draw out seven buckets from it, except if the water has changed, in which case draw it out until it becomes clean. If a dog falls into it and you are able to draw out its water, then do so. And everything that falls into the well that has no blood, like the scorpion, the beetles, and the likes of that — there is no problem.'

key_terms.دِلَاء: plural of dalw — a bucket or vessel used for drawing water from a well
key_terms.لَيْسَ لَهُ دَمٌ: has no flowing blood — the key criterion distinguishing ritually significant from non-significant contamination
key_terms.يَطِيبَ: to become wholesome/pure — indicating restoration of ritual purity
key_terms.يُنْزَحُ: to draw/scoop out water from a well — the technical jurisprudential term for purifying a well

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on a well when a rat or dog falls into it?
ai.summary: Abu Basir asked Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) about the ruling on wells when animals fall into them. The Imam gave a graduated ruling: for small animals like rats, seven buckets must be drawn; if a dog falls in, all the water must be drawn if possible; but for creatures lacking flowing blood — scorpions, beetles, and similar insects — there is no issue. This ruling reflects early Shia jurisprudence's careful approach to taharah (ritual purity) of water sources, distinguishing between bloodied mammals and bloodless invertebrates.
